title: A source ledger for brief, proposal and verified outcome
description: A source ledger separates a brief, a proposal and a verified outcome.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A source ledger separates a brief, a proposal and a verified outcome. This prevents an attractive concept image from being promoted into evidence of completed work.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Give each source a stable reference and record what it actually supports. Label proposed ideas, approved specifications and observed outcomes differently. Keep private documents out of public captions. Link each factual sentence in a proposed story to its source before publication.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A proposal may establish the intended arrangement but not prove installation. A dated, permitted installation photograph answers a different question.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What stage does the source document?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: A source label is not verification by itself. Genuine project claims need actual evidence and permission; concepts remain concepts.

title: Distinguishing an actual installation from a concept scene
description: An actual installation and a concept scene can look equally convincing on a screen.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: An actual installation and a concept scene can look equally convincing on a screen. The label and source are therefore essential parts of how the image is understood.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Look for an explicit disclosure and a source record. Describe a concept as a visualization used to explore an idea. For a genuine installation story, require project-specific evidence and permission. Avoid adding a customer, location or completion date merely to make a caption feel complete.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A table pictured beside a mountain view may be a useful room-composition reference. It is not evidence that the atelier installed a table in that location.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What is the image classified as?
Which claim would go beyond it?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Do not infer real-world events from photorealism. A concept does not count as a completed customer project.

title: Why a detail photograph needs a wider context
description: A detail photograph needs context so the reader understands what it is a detail of.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A detail photograph needs context so the reader understands what it is a detail of. This is especially important when several related forms appear in one project or concept.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Pair the detail with a labelled wider view where available. Identify the area shown without inventing hidden construction. Explain why the detail matters to the story. If the wider view is unavailable, state that limit instead of implying a complete visual record.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A close-up of a blue edge can explain a colour boundary, but it cannot show the object's full proportions or room placement.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Several details do not create several projects. Keep all views tied to the same source identity where appropriate.

title: Choosing images that explain a design decision
description: A project image should earn its place by explaining something.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A project image should earn its place by explaining something. Selecting by visual attractiveness alone can leave the actual design decision unclear.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Write the decision in one sentence, then choose the image that helps a reader understand it. Add a second view only if it contributes different information. Label concepts and verified photographs accurately. Keep private or identifying details out unless their publication is permitted.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A wider image may explain the relationship to seating, while a close-up explains an edge transition. Two nearly identical angles may add little.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Which decision does each image explain?
What new information does the second view add?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Image selection cannot supply missing evidence about a customer, material property or completed installation.

title: A project caption that says only what is known
description: A trustworthy caption says what is known and leaves unknowns open.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A trustworthy caption says what is known and leaves unknowns open. Specificity should come from evidence, not from a desire to make the story sound complete.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: List the visible subject, the source classification and the reason it is shown. Check any name, location, date or material claim against its source and permission. Remove details that cannot be supported. Keep private evidence in the register, not in the public caption.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: “Concept room study exploring a blue accent beside brown grain-like lines” describes an intention without inventing a client, timber species or installation.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: A filename or visual resemblance is not enough to verify a factual claim. When uncertain, use narrower wording.

title: What genuine before-and-after evidence requires
description: Before-and-after imagery makes a claim about a change.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Before-and-after imagery makes a claim about a change. It needs evidence that the images concern the same subject and that their sequence and context are accurate.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Record the source, date and subject identity for both images. Explain relevant differences in viewpoint or lighting. Confirm permission for the proposed use. State the actual change without attributing causes that the evidence cannot establish.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A concept rendering beside a different room photograph is not a verified before-and-after pair. It can be shown as a proposal comparison only with a clear explanation.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Does the caption accurately describe the comparison?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Do not manufacture an outcome by pairing unrelated images or treating a visualization as the “after” photograph.

title: Understanding customer attribution choices
description: Public attribution is a choice that needs a recorded scope.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Public attribution is a choice that needs a recorded scope. A customer's private identity and the name permitted on a website may be different.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Keep the original feedback source private. Record the exact public attribution approved for the intended use. Check whether images, location details or a longer story have separate permissions. Review the final public presentation against those limits.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: Permission to use initials with a quote does not automatically authorize a full name, portrait or location in a related card.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Does the final presentation stay within that scope?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Do not invent an attribution to fill a design. Fictional samples must remain labelled and unattributed as customer feedback.

title: Separating a testimonial from a marketing headline
description: A testimonial is a sourced account from a real person; a marketing headline is editorial wording.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A testimonial is a sourced account from a real person; a marketing headline is editorial wording. Keeping them distinct prevents promotional language from being mistaken for customer evidence.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Preserve the original quote and its private source. Compare any edited version against the meaning and allowed use. Keep editorial headings outside quotation marks and clearly separate from the testimony. If a statement is fictional, disclose that prominently before the text.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A heading such as “A considered process” can introduce a topic, but it should not be styled as a customer's quote unless the source actually said it and publication is permitted.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Which words come from the source?
Is permission recorded for the exact public use?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: No rating, identity or customer experience should be generated to strengthen a testimonial. Translations remain the same feedback record.

title: Following related reading without repeating the same story
description: Related reading should add a new question or perspective.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Related reading should add a new question or perspective. Repeating the same story under another title makes an archive harder to navigate.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Compare the purpose of the current entry with each proposed related link. Choose a link that answers a next question, supplies context or explains a limit. Record why it is related. Avoid creating new entries solely to hold another image or translation of the same story.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A room-photography worksheet can lead to an access-measurement guide because it advances the brief. Another nearly identical photography article may not.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What new question does the link answer?
Does it repeat the current entry?
Is the relationship clear to the reader?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: A related link does not establish that the records describe the same real project. Keep identities and classifications distinct.

title: An image-by-image permission ledger for a public case study
description: An image-by-image permission ledger makes public use easier to review.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: An image-by-image permission ledger makes public use easier to review. Different images in one story may have different sources, subjects and allowed uses.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Assign each image a stable reference. Record its source, classification, proposed caption, identifying details and permission scope. Link approval to the exact version selected. Keep the ledger private while exposing only the approved caption and disclosure publicly.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A permitted object photograph and an unapproved room photograph should not inherit the same status merely because they sit in one folder.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Folder access is not proof of publication rights. Unknown permission remains pending, and concepts still need truthful classification.
